items.q: Design Uber-style live location tracking and sharing
shortAnswer: Uber-style live location sharing: a publisher's position streams to many watchers in near real time, with consent, background updates, and battery constraints.
Model it as session publish-subscribe: adaptive accuracy driven by foreground or background state, a battery-aware upload cadence, and push-plus-pull fan-out to watchers.
Probes target background location — the ongoing-notification consent contract — staleness UX, server-side ETA so watchers agree, and geofence checks that survive app kill.
items.prompt:
Design live location tracking and sharing (a driver ETA product / Find-My-Friends): users see each other's positions moving on a map, with consent, background updates, and battery constraints.

Assume tens of millions of users, Android + iOS, and location must keep updating while the app is in the background. **Set a 45-minute timer and talk out loud.** Tick the requirements as you genuinely cover them.
items.framework: Two hard systems in one: on-device **location lifecycle** (accuracy vs battery) and a **server fan-out** problem (many watchers per publisher). Run the two-phase framework; interviewers probe battery/background handling and the live-update path hardest.
requirements: Define the on-device location pipeline (GPS, fused, accuracy modes)
Design background location with Android restrictions
Design the upload policy: how often, batching, batching under weak signal
Design the live-update path: push to all watchers
Design the server: ingestion, session state, fan-out
Handle the ETA estimation input (speed, history)
Handle stale or no GPS (cached last known, interpolation)
Address battery and data cost explicitly
Design consent, privacy, and revocation
Cover cold-start of a sharing session
Design the geofence use case (arrival alert)
Mention how accuracy differs by UI state (foreground map vs background)
Close with explicit trade-offs
items.referenceAnswer:
#### Model
A publisher (the tracked user) runs a **session**; watchers subscribe to it. The core payload is a position fix `{ lat, lng, accuracy, heading, speed, ts }` plus a session lifecycle event (started/ended/paused). Publish-subscribe is per-session: a session id with a watcher list. `Publisher device ──publish──> LocationIngest ──> session store ──> push fan-out ──> watcher devices`.

#### On-device location
Use the fused location provider with adaptive accuracy: **foreground UI visible → high accuracy (GPS + network), background → low power** (network + battery saver). The foreground/background switch is driven by app lifecycle + a foreground service holding a `location` type while sharing is active. Android requires the user-facing “ongoing” notification for background location — that is not a bug, it is the platform's consent contract and the product should embrace it.

#### Upload policy
Server-adaptive and battery-aware: at rest → 30–60 s cadence; moving with speed > threshold → 5–10 s; low battery → back off to 5 minutes. Batch multiple fixes per request. Under weak signal, buffer and send a delta of positions on reconnect. This is the “distance since last upload” heuristic.

#### Fan-out
Each update fans out to the watcher set. Two delivery tiers: **active watchers** (map is on screen) get a push (FCM data message) and then pull the fix; **passive watchers** just get the ETA on an interval. Push + pull hybrid: push tells the client “a new fix exists”, the client fetches it, which keeps the wire format simple and lets the server batch. For a live map, a WebSocket/persistent connection tier is the right call at scale, with pushes as the heartbeat.

#### ETA
Computed server-side from recent speed samples and route — client displays the server's ETA so all watchers agree. Never estimate purely on the client; the server has the history.

#### Staleness & correctness
Every fix carries a server timestamp. Watchers show age: green < 15 s, amber < 60 s, grey beyond. If GPS is lost, the client reports the last known fix + `gpsLost: true` and interpolation is done client-side for smoothness only, never for ETA.

#### Consent & privacy
Sharing is opt-in per watcher or per group, revocable instantly. Revocation stops publishing immediately and the session ends server-side. The consent record is auditable; the location payload is stored with a short TTL (not mined). Only the current fix is fanned out — no historical path is kept by default (a decision the product can override for trip receipts).

#### Failure modes
Bad GPS indoors → fused provider + WiFi scan. Server down → clients keep publishing locally and replay on reconnect; watchers show stale. Battery death → last known + 'stopped updating' flag. Cross-timezone clocks → use server timestamps throughout.

shortAnswer: An offline-first news reader: articles work on a plane, bookmarks and read-state sync across devices, and offline is first-class, not degraded.
Local storage owns read-state, the network owns content: Room holds articles and monotonic mutation log, with delta sync, push freshness, and bounded image caching.
Grading centers on the local-first inversion, a monotonic last-write-wins conflict policy — no CRDT for tiny toggle fields — prefetch budgets, and offline-coverage metrics.
items.prompt:
Design an offline-first news reader: articles are available on a plane, content is fresh when online, bookmarks and read-state sync across devices, and edits to read-state never conflict badly.

Assume ~50M MAU, a shared content feed, and that 'offline' must be a first-class state, not a degraded one. **Set a 45-minute timer and talk out loud.** Tick the requirements as you genuinely cover them.
items.framework: The canonical local-first scenario. Run the two-phase framework; in Phase 2 the interviewer wants to see **local as the source of truth** (see sd-0017) plus a freshness strategy, plus a conflict-resolution policy for tiny per-item writes.
requirements: Design the offline content model (article, metadata, images)
Design the fetch-ahead policy: what gets prefetched and when
Design the sync model: full refresh vs delta vs push
Design conflict resolution for read-state and bookmarks
Handle the freshness contract: staleness, 'updated on disk' timestamps
Design image caching offline (bounded disk, eviction)
Handle the online/offline transition cleanly
Design multi-device convergence of bookmarks and history
Cover first-run onboarding vs returning user
Address bandwidth and storage budgets
Design a way to measure offline quality (coverage of 'offline opened' vs 'online opened')
Mention how new articles reach the client without a full poll
Close with explicit trade-offs
items.referenceAnswer:
#### Local-first framing
**Local storage is the source of truth for read-state; the network is the source of truth for content.** Every article read is written to Room immediately; the 'unread' badge reads Room, not the server. This inverts the classic architecture and is the whole point of the design — offline is not a fallback, it is the primary path.

#### Content model
`Article { id, sectionId, title, body, imageRefs[], publishedAt }` in a Room DB, with an FTS index for search (sk-00xx). Image files live in a disk cache, referenced by URL hash, so the DB never stores blobs. Read-state is `ArticleState { id, readAt?, bookmarked?, progressPercent? }`, per-device but synced.

#### Prefetch / fetch-ahead
On connect (or via push “new issue”), the client fetches the section manifest + the top N articles per section (body as one payload, images separate, lazy). A background worker on unmetered WiFi + charging downloads the full issue — 'magazine mode'. The manifest carries sizes so the client can budget: 'this issue is 40 MB, download images only on WiFi'.

#### Sync
Deltas, not full refreshes: the client sends `since <lastSyncedAt>` and the server replies with changed ids. New content arrives via FCM topic push ('issue 42 is ready') plus a periodic reconciliation for missed pushes. Outbound: read-state is a small, monotonic log of mutations, replayed to the server; the server merges by last-write-wins per field with the client's clock, but read-state is *monotonic* (unread → read never reverts) so conflicts are trivial.

#### Conflict resolution
The dangerous field is 'bookmarked' (toggle-able). Policy: **LWW on the server timestamp**, with a small reconciliation window — if two devices write conflicting values within a day, keep the newer server ts and show the user a merge hint once. `progressPercent` uses max, never min. This is far simpler than CRDTs because the per-item state is tiny and toggle-heavy; a CRDT is over-engineering here (unlike sd-0018).

#### Online/offline transition
A single `ConnectivityManager` + network-quality gate drives the sync worker. The client exposes state as a `Flow<SyncState>`; the UI shows 'Offline — you'll get 42 new articles when back online'. No screen is blocked by connectivity.

#### Image budget
Disk cache sized to ~10% of free space, LRU eviction, `isOfflineEligible` only for prefetched images. Images are never required for reading text; tapping an image shows a loader if it missed.

#### Measurement
The north-star is **offline coverage** = 'articles opened while offline' / 'articles opened'. Everything else (sync lag, conflict rate) is secondary. You tune prefetch depth until coverage is high enough.

#### Trade-offs
Local-first costs storage and sync complexity but buys instant UI and airplane reliability. Prefetching a magazine costs bandwidth; make it opt-in. Monotonic LWW is simple but can't express 'sibling' edits — acceptable here because per-field state is small.

items.q: Design push notifications at scale on FCM
shortAnswer: Push at scale on FCM: campaigns to millions, daily digests, and transactional alerts, where delivery rate and opt-out rate are the numbers that matter.
Separate delivery urgency from display: transactional, campaign, and digest queues; run token lifecycle as a feedback loop and fan out in waves with dead-lettering.
Interviewers push on token freshness and pruning, per-user throttling with local-time scheduling, client-side mute rules before posting, and ack-versus-receipt analytics.
items.prompt:
Design a push-notification service built on FCM: campaign pushes to millions, personalized daily digests, transactional alerts, and the on-device handling that makes the product not annoying.

Assume ~50M devices, multiple push campaigns per week, and that delivery rate and opt-out rate are the two numbers that matter. **Set a 45-minute timer and talk out loud.** Tick the requirements as you genuinely cover them.
items.framework: Half infrastructure (scheduling, batching, retries, token lifecycle), half product discipline (throttling, user-visible channel design). Run the two-phase framework; interviewers probe token freshness and the 'not annoying' layer — opt-outs kill the product.
requirements: Design the token lifecycle: registration, refresh, invalidation
Design the scheduler for campaigns (who, when, throttling)
Design the send pipeline: batching, fan-out, retries
Handle FCM's delivery contract: data vs notification messages, priority
Design the on-device receiving and display policy
Design digest aggregation and time-of-day batching
Handle geographic/local time delivery
Design unsubscribe, mute, and quiet-hours
Cover delivery analytics: FCM ack vs on-device receipt
Design the rate-limiter for a campaign over millions
Handle multiple devices per user
Mention the cold-start no-network case
Close with explicit trade-offs
items.referenceAnswer:
#### Push types
The contract must separate delivery urgency from display: **transactional** (OTP, payment — deliver fast, display loud), **campaign** (newsletter-ish — batch, throttled, quiet), **digest** (aggregated, at a chosen local time). One pipeline, three queues with different SLA and throttle settings.

#### Token lifecycle
FCM gives each app install a token that changes on reinstall, restore, and after long inactivity. The client reports the token to our registry on every launch; the registry marks a token stale if it doesn't see the device in N days, and FCM's `unregistered` response on send prunes it. Token hygiene is a feedback loop: prune rate is a metric, not an afterthought.

#### Scheduler
A campaign = a targeting query (segment, e.g. 'active in 30d, not muted') evaluated against the profile store → a list of `(device, local_time)` tuples. Delivery is spread over hours and localized to the user's timezone — a global launch at 09:00 UTC is a 09:00 local launch for everyone. Per-user throttling: max N pushes/day, cooldown between pushes, quiet-hours respected. This is where opt-out rate is won or lost.

#### Send pipeline
Fan-out in waves (100k at a time) through FCM with per-batch backoff; a message queue holds the fan-out so a spike doesn't melt the sender. Use **data messages** (not notification messages) for campaign content so the app decides display — needed for digests and muting. Transactional uses high-priority data or notification messages per SLA.

#### Retries & dead-letter
FCM failures: transient → retry with exponential backoff; `UnregisteredError` → drop the token and mark the device stale; invalid payload → dead-letter to a quarantine queue for operator review. No unbounded retry on campaign pushes — they have a delivery window.

#### On-device policy
The app receives the push (data message → a NotificationManager post). The client applies the mute/quiet-hours/channel rules *before* posting — never post then cancel, the flicker is worse. Channels (per product area) let the OS carry user intent. A settings screen writes to Room; the client also reports the effective mute state to the registry so the server can skip sends.

#### Digests
Daily digest = aggregate N stories/alerts into one notification at a user-chosen time. Server-side aggregation at generation, delivered once — cheaper than N sends and dramatically less annoying.

#### Analytics
Two layers: **FCM ack** (FCM accepted and forwarded — delivery proxy) and **on-device receipt** (app actually received and displayed). The gap is 'FCM silent drops', measured by comparing the two. Success metrics: delivery rate, open rate, and the guarded one — **opt-out rate**, tied to a throttling dashboard with rollback.

#### Failure modes
Cold start offline → pushes are delivered by the OS later, no work needed. Token storm after a reinstall wave → registry must handle bursty registration. FCM outage → queue and retry, and the throttling dashboard pauses campaigns. Multiple devices per user → send once per device, mute on any.

items.q: Design modularization for a large Android app
shortAnswer: Split a 15-plus-minute monolith into buildable, ownable modules for ~200 engineers across 40 teams, without blowing up build times or creating dependency hell.
Layers: `:app` shell, `:feature:*`, `:domain`, `:core:*`, `:libs:*`. Ban feature-to-feature deps; split `api()`/`implementation()` with lint.
Grading focuses on build-time engineering — configuration caching, remote build cache, release-only R8 — plus a bottom-up migration that stays green and enforced acyclicity.
items.prompt:
Design the module structure for an app with ~200 engineers across 40 teams: split a monolith into buildable, ownable modules without blowing up build times or creating dependency hell.

Assume an existing large app that builds in 15+ minutes, circular dependencies, and no enforced boundaries. **Set a 45-minute timer and talk out loud.** Tick the requirements as you genuinely cover them.
items.framework: This is more of an architecture/process scenario than a runtime design. Run the two-phase framework; the interviewer wants dependency-structure thinking (layering, direction, cycles) plus build-time engineering (Gradle, incremental builds, remote cache).
requirements: Define the module layering (core → domain → feature → app)
Define the ownership and API-boundary rules
Design the dependency rules and how cycles are prevented
Design the build-time strategy: R8/Room/KSP tasks, Gradle cache, task configuration
Handle the code-path: how features depend on other features
Design the app shell and feature discovery
Design how shared UI and design system is modularized
Address the migration path from a monolith
Design the enforcement: lint rules, architecture tests, CI gates
Handle analytics and A/B instrumentation across features
Cover testing at each layer and the test-fixture pattern
Mention version catalogs and dependency management

items.referenceAnswer:
#### Why modularize
Three goals that trade against each other: **build time** (fewer modules → fewer tasks), **ownership** (more modules → clearer boundaries), **testing** (isolated unit tests). The design must make the trade-off explicit per layer.

#### Layering
The classic shape, top-down dependency direction: `:app (shell) ──> :feature:* ──> :domain:* ──> :core:* (ui, datastore, network) ──> :libs:*`. Every dependency points downward. `:core:*` never depends on a `:feature:*`. `:domain` is pure Kotlin (no Android) so it compiles in milliseconds and tests in milliseconds — this is the fastest module in the graph and the one that carries the business rules.

#### Feature modules
One module per feature, owned by one team. **No feature-to-feature dependency** — a feature that needs another's data talks to it through `:domain` interfaces or an event bus, or the consuming feature depends on the producer's *contract* module. This is the rule that prevents cycles and makes the graph a DAG that CI can verify.

#### API boundaries
Each module exports an `api()` vs `implementation()` split: implementation deps stay private. Public API is reviewed like a public contract — an `@InternalApi` annotation + a strict-API lint rule that fails a build if a non-public class leaks into `api()`.

#### Build time
The two things that make big builds slow: configuration phase (thousands of tasks to evaluate) and non-incremental tasks (KSP, R8, Room). Mitigations: build-time configuration caching, Gradle remote build cache (share compiled classes across CI and devs), task-level input normalization, and **pushing R8 down to release-only** so dev builds skip it. Feature isolation means a change in `:feature:payments` rebuilds that module + dependents, not the whole app — the payoff of the DAG.

#### The app shell
`:app` is thin: it owns DI wiring (or delegates to a `:app:di` module), navigation graph composition, and feature registration. Features register via a navigator interface or a lightweight service locator in the shell; no feature references another feature's activity class directly.

#### Design system
A `:ui:design-system` module (tokens, components, theme) that everything depends on. It must be stable: an API freeze with a review process, because its change blast radius is the whole app.

#### Migration
Extract bottom-up: start with `:core:network`, then `:domain`, then the smallest feature — each extraction is a separate PR that keeps the build green. A migration badge per module ('in monolith' → 'extracted') tracked in a dashboard. The monolith keeps compiling during extraction; you don't do a big-bang rewrite.

#### Enforcement
The design is only real if enforced: an architecture test (like ArchUnit) that fails on upward or cross-feature dependencies, a lint rule that flags `api()` leaks, a CI check that the module graph is acyclic, and a `gradle buildHealth` command that reports per-module build times to catch a module that's quietly becoming a second monolith.

shortAnswer: Offline maps with turn-by-turn navigation: download a region, browse and navigate without a network, with voice prompts and rerouting on constrained devices.

items.referenceAnswer:
#### The data model — vector tiles
The core decision: store **vector tiles**, not rasters. A vector tile is compact geometry (roads, buildings, labels) per zoom level; it renders at device DPI and memory is a fraction of a raster. A region of a metro area is ~50–200 MB of vector tiles vs 10x that in raster. Rendering is done on-device with a tile pipeline that caches decoded geometry.

#### Region download
The user picks a region (draw a box / city preset). The client computes the tile set at zoom levels 0–16, estimates size from a server-provided size table, and streams it with pause/resume and partial-apply (a region is only 'live' when its index is complete). Budgets: 'this region needs 300 MB, you have 500 MB free'. The metadata index (tile offsets, a name-to-tile lookup) is a small SQLite DB — queries on it power browse and search.

#### Storage layout
Tile files in a read-mostly container + a SQLite index. LRU eviction with region semantics (evict whole tiles, never half a region). Free-space check before download. A 'map on device' list with per-region size and update status.

#### Routing
The graph (nodes/edges with weights) is embedded in the tiles. **Precomputed routing data at region-download time**: contraction hierarchies (CH) built server-side and shipped with the region give sub-second routing on mid-range phones. The route engine is pure Kotlin, runs off the main thread, and caches the last route. **Reroute offline**: if the driver deviates, recompute on-device (same CH) — fast enough for 'off route' recovery without the network. When online, traffic weights update the graph and a live route is preferred, with a graceful 'traffic data lost' message.

#### Search
Geocoding offline = reverse index in the region DB (POI names, street names) + tokenized fuzzy match. Results are region-scoped ('city + area'). Address search quality is the '10% feature' that costs 50% of the effort — be honest that offline search is a degraded, bounded experience.

#### Voice
TTS runs on-device; prompt generation (maneuver → 'turn right on Elm in 300 m') is a rule engine fed by the route geometry and current position — no network, no latency. Audio focus and volume ducking are UX requirements.

#### Navigation sensors
Location with `LocationRequest` at high accuracy while navigating; bearing from a fused GPS + gyro + magnetometer; a dead-reckoning fallback in tunnels (last known velocity extrapolation) with a 'GPS lost' banner. Prompt timing: compute distance-to-maneuver against the route geometry, trigger at ~300 m, repeat with a countdown, recalc after each fix.

#### Battery & memory
Navigation runs a foreground service; screen-on is the big drain, so the renderer caps at ~30 fps and dims. Tile decode is cached; geometry is not re-decoded each frame. On a long trip, memory stays flat — a leak here kills the app mid-drive.

#### Trade-offs
Vector tiles cost a tile-pipeline build but save storage and enable high-DPI rendering. Precomputed CH routing costs download size but gives fast offline reroute. Offline search is bounded and that's a product decision to be explicit about.
